hints: Think about what ions are free in solution when soluble MBr2 meets soluble AgNO3, and which combination forms an insoluble salt.
Recall the three silver halide colours in order: chloride is white, bromide is in the middle, iodide is yellow.
walkthrough:
Spot the precipitating pair**
You have $\text{Br}^{-}$ from $\text{MBr}_{2}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{Ag}^{+}$ from $\text{AgNO}_{3}(\text{aq})$. Silver bromides are insoluble, while all nitrates and Group 2 bromides are soluble, so $\text{Ag}^{+}$ and $\text{Br}^{-}$ join to form solid $\text{AgBr}$.

Remember the exact cream shade**
Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream (pale off white) and silver iodide is yellow. For bromide you must write cream, not white and not yellow.

Final answer: Formula: $\text{AgBr}$
Colour: cream

hints: Start from the insoluble product identified in (a) and pair the remaining ions, M2+ and NO3-, to find the other product.
walkthrough:
Balance by matching Br and Ag**
Each $\text{MBr}_{2}$ supplies two $\text{Br}^{-}$ ions, so you need two $\text{Ag}^{+}$ ions to precipitate both as $2\text{AgBr}$. That means two $\text{AgNO}_{3}$ on the left, leaving two $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ to join $\text{M}^{2+}$ as $\text{M(NO}_{3})_{2}$ on the right: $$\text{MBr}_{2} + 2\text{AgNO}_{3} \rightarrow 2\text{AgBr} + \text{M(NO}_{3})_{2}$$

hints: Link mass and moles to relative formula mass using $M_{r} = mass \div moles$.
Subtract the mass contributed by the two bromide ions from $M_{r}$ of MBr2 to leave the atomic mass of M.
Match your value for the atomic mass of M to the closest Group 2 metal in the Periodic Table.
walkthrough:
Calculate Mr from mass and moles**
Relative formula mass is mass of one mole. Use: $$M_{r} = \frac{m}{n} = \frac{0.250}{8.415 \times 10^{-4}} = 297.1$$ Keep one decimal place here to allow accurate subtraction next.

Strip out the two bromines**
$M_{r}(\text{MBr}_{2}) = A_{r}(\text{M}) + 2A_{r}(\text{Br})$. With $A_{r}(\text{Br}) = 79.9$: $$A_{r}(\text{M}) = 297.1 - (2 \times 79.9) = 297.1 - 159.8 = 137.3$$

Name the Group 2 metal**
An $A_{r}$ near 137 in Group 2 is barium, Ba. This fits because Ba is a Group 2 metal that forms $\text{BaBr}_{2}$.

hints: Think about which halogen is more reactive, chlorine or bromine, and what coloured element is released into solution.
walkthrough:
Picture chlorine pushing bromine out**
Chlorine is above bromine in Group 17, so it is the stronger oxidising agent. It oxidises colourless $\text{Br}^{-}$ to $\text{Br}_{2}$: $$\text{Cl}_{2} + 2\text{Br}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^{-} + \text{Br}_{2}$$ Dissolved bromine gives the familiar orange to brown colour.
Final answer: Solution turns colourless to orange / brown due to $\text{Br}_{2}$ formed.

hints: Recall the name given when a more reactive halogen takes the place of a less reactive halide in solution.
walkthrough:
Name the halogen swap**
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its halide. Here chlorine displaces bromine, so this is a displacement reaction, also accepted as redox.

hints: For an insoluble solid you cannot use aqueous AgNO3 directly, so think of the single acid that both releases HX gas and then oxidises it.
Recall the specific colour of the vapour produced when bromide is oxidised to bromine by the hot acid.
walkthrough:
Choose the acid that tests solids**
Add concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ directly to solid Y. It first releases $\text{HBr}$ gas, then as an oxidising agent it oxidises $\text{Br}^{-}$ to $\text{Br}_{2}$.

Link bromide to brown bromine**
Chloride would give only colourless fumes, iodide would give black solid plus purple vapour, but bromide gives steamy fumes plus brown $\text{Br}_{2}$ vapour. Seeing brown vapour confirms bromide.

Final answer: reagent: concentrated sulfuric acid
observation: brown vapour / gas forms

hints: Compare which of the three solids can break down on heating to release a gas, and what that means for the mass left in the test tube.
Recall the unique coloured gas released when a nitrate decomposes.
Think about why MgO, already an oxide, shows no further change on strong heating.
walkthrough:
Use mass loss to narrow down**
Heat each 1.0 g sample strongly. $\text{MgCO}_{3} \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{CO}_{2}$ and $2\text{Mg(NO}_{3})_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{MgO} + 4\text{NO}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$ both release gases, so the solid residue weighs less than 1.0 g. $\text{MgO}$ is already the stable oxide, so its mass stays at 1.0 g.

Use brown fumes to pick out the nitrate**
Only the nitrate decomposition produces brown $\text{NO}_{2}$ gas. The carbonate releases only colourless $\text{CO}_{2}$. So brown fumes identify $\text{Mg(NO}_{3})_{2}$.

Confirm MgO by no change**
The sample that shows no visible change and no mass loss on strong heating must be $\text{MgO}$.

Final answer: Both $\text{MgCO}_{3}$ and $\text{Mg(NO}_{3})_{2}$ lose mass / mass less than 1.0 g after heating due to gas loss.
$\text{Mg(NO}_{3})_{2}$ gives brown $\text{NO}_{2}$ fumes, $\text{MgCO}_{3}$ does not.
$\text{MgO}$ shows no reaction / no change in mass.

hints: Start from Mg atom 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 and remove the outer shell electrons to form Mg2+.
walkthrough:
Remove the 3s electrons**
Mg is $1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{2}$. The $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ cation has lost the two $3s$ electrons, leaving the stable neon structure: $$1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}$$

hints: Think about what you see when any white magnesium solid dissolves in dilute acid to give soluble MgCl2.
Think about which anion produces a gas with H+ and which simply forms water.
walkthrough:
Spot the common dissolving**
Both reactions are acid base neutralisations forming soluble $\text{MgCl}_{2}$: $$\text{MgCO}_{3} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_{2} + \text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ $$\text{Mg(OH)}_{2} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ In both cases the white solid disappears to leave a colourless solution.

Use fizzing to tell them apart**
Only carbonate releases $\text{CO}_{2}$ gas, seen as fizzing or effervescence. The hydroxide only makes water, so it dissolves quietly with no bubbles.

Final answer: similarity: both solids disappear / dissolve to give colourless solution
difference: $\text{MgCO}_{3}$ fizzes / effervescence due to $\text{CO}_{2}$, $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$ shows no fizzing
